title: Heap priming latency scratch
body:
Quick context:
- Goal: test if explicit heap priming (allocating and touching KV and attention buffers ahead of request burst) reduces cold-to-warm tail latency for short chat-turn workloads (~32–128 tokens).
- Hypothesis: A small, deterministic priming routine that runs on instance spin-up or just before an expected burst can reduce p95/p99 by avoiding on-path lazy allocations and cold page faults.

Notes (high-level):
- Environment: dedicated GPU instance (A100, 80GB), Ubuntu 22.04, runtime build: pr/2784 (minor allocator changes + priming hook).
- Client harness: rps-play (home-grown), reproducible arrival patterns: stepped-ramp (0 -> 200 rps over 60s), impulse (burst 500 rps for 8s), Poisson baseline (200 rps mean). Payloads: small prompt ~40 tokens; generation 32 tokens; beamless sampling.
- Measurement: p50/p90/p95/p99, cold-start first 60s, steady-state aggregated over 5min windows. Each experiment repeated 3x; median reported.

Priming procedure implemented (sketch):
- Allocate prefetch buffers: kv-cache reserve for max-beam-size and max-seqlen (here: 1 * 2048 * 4 bytes approx).
- Touch pages: sequential write of a 1MB stride to force kernel page fault handling.
- Warm tokenizer: run tokenization on a 256k dummy payload to instantiate subroutines.
- Dummy forward: run a 1-step forward with extremely small batch (1) to ensure CUDA kernels are JIT-compiled / warmed (where applicable) and cublas/cuDNN paths are cold-resolved.
- Hook placed in: instance start and on scheduled pre-burst signal.

Experiment matrix (short):
- A: baseline (no priming)
- B: priming at start (one-time during init)
- C: priming immediately before each burst (pre-burst hook)
- D: priming + lightweight periodic top-up (every 30s)

Representative run (impulse burst, 500rps for 8s):
- Baseline A (median of 3 runs):
  p50=22ms, p90=48ms, p95=85ms, p99=210ms, first-10s spike: many >300ms
- Priming at start B:
  p50=20ms, p90=40ms, p95=72ms, p99=160ms, first-10s spike reduced but still present (~220ms)
- Pre-burst priming C:
  p50=19ms, p90=36ms, p95=65ms, p99=120ms, first-10s spike mostly removed (max ~150ms)
- Periodic top-up D:
  p50=19ms, p90=35ms, p95=62ms, p99=115ms, steady state slightly improved vs C

Observations:
- The single priming-at-start helps, but does not fully prevent spikes if instance has been idle for minutes. Some OS-level reclamation + cuda context inactivity seems to reintroduce penalty.
- Pre-burst priming (run ~5s before expected burst) is more effective; it aligns allocations/compilation to the request timeline so first-wave gets warm kernels and resident pages.
- Periodic top-up slightly better but adds CPU overhead (~0.4% CPU) — acceptable for dedicated tier, questionable for constrained multi-tenant.
- The dominant source of p99 in baseline is page faults + lazy GPU context initialization + occasional allocator stalls inside our runtime memory pool.

Quick ascii timeline (single impulse run, p95 trace):
Time(s) | Baseline p95 | Pre-burst p95
0-8     | 180–220ms    | 60–90ms
9-16    | 80–100ms     | 40–60ms

Commands / harness snippets used:
- rps-play --model rwd-small --qps 500 --pattern impulse --burst 8 --prompt-file small.json --out results/burst-A.json
- ./priming_hook --touch-pages 128 --dummy-forward --tok-prime --log priming.log

Micro-profiling (observed hotspots):
- slow path: my_allocator::grow_pool -> mutex wait (rare but expensive)
- cuda: first cuLaunchKernel reported ~100–200ms extra on cold wave (JIT/cubin load).
- tokenizer: first Tokenizer::init does file mapping and plausible one-time cost.

Ideas & next steps:
- Move priming to a lightweight background thread that performs page touches and a tokenization warm run but defers the dummy forward until a pre-burst signal (safer cpu/gpu balance).
- Investigate making allocator growth lockless or pre-reserve for common instance sizes (avoid in-request growth path).
- Add a metric: time-since-last-priming to telemetry and correlate with p99.
- Try a variant where priming is done by a colocated warmup worker process (isolates allocation noise).
- Evaluate cost: CPU overhead vs latency benefit (compute cost per % p99 improvement).

Open questions / anomalies:
- On one run priming seemed to increase p95 by ~10ms for the first 30s (likely due to priming work contenting with requests). Need to test priming scheduling (priority niceness).
- Are there kernel module interactions causing page reclamation after a minute of idleness? Need to check VM overcommit and kernel logs.

Short conclusion (working):
- Explicit heap priming significantly reduces first-wave tail latency for sudden bursts. Best results when priming is timed shortly before burst. Production rollout should weigh CPU overhead vs SLO improvements; a conservative approach: pre-burst priming for dedicated and canary lane, periodic top-up optional.

TODOs:
- [ ] Add time-since-last-priming telemetry (ENGINF-4821).
- [ ] Benchmark priming CPU cost across instance sizes (small/medium/large).
- [ ] Add unit that runs priming at canary scale and monitor user-facing error budgets for 48h.
- [ ] Follow up: allocator growth refactor - reduce lock hold times.

Notes to self: schedule a quick demo for SRE on Wed 11/13 — show before/after plots and the priming hook code (pr/2784).
